Acting Attorney General a member of Sessions’s staff who had not been 
confirmed to any position in the Trump Administration. Trump rehed on a 
statutory provision that entitled him to name as the Acting Attorney 
General any employee of the Justice Department who had served in the 
department for at least 90 days and whose pay grade was at least 
equivalent to that of a GS-15 official. Trump bypassed Deputy Attorney 
General Rod Rosenstein, whose supervision of the Special Counsel 
investigation into the 2016 election had drawn Trump’s criticism, in favor 
of Matthew Whitaker, Attorney General Sessions’s chief of staff. What was 
unusual was not the designation of a non-confirmed acting agency head— 
such temporary appointments are common during the early days of a new 
Administration—^but rather the designation of a non-confirmed acting 
agency head not rendered necessary by the inauguration of a new 
president.
The Whitaker appointment triggered a number of legal challenges 
arguing that, under Buckley v. Valeo, he could not constitutionally function 
as the Justice Department’s "principal officer.” For its part, OLC had 
opined that an Acting Attorney General was not, in fact, a principal officer, 
and that the President’s designation of Mr. Whitaker was permissible 
because he had been permissibly appointed by a previous head of the 
Department to be an inferior officer. Designating an Acting Attorney Gen,, 
2018 WL 6131923 (O.L.C. Nov. 14, 2018). To support the proposition that 
an acting department head should not be deemed a principal officer, OLC 
relied on a combination of early Supreme Court cases, as well as the history 
of executive branch practice—citing in support of its argument the 
executive branch “defeat” in Noel Canning. The few trial courts to reach 
the issue during Whitaker’s tenure agreed that he was an inferior officer 
by virtue of the temporary nature of his appointment. Guedes v. Bureau of 
Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, & Explosives, 356 F. Supp. 3d 109, 146 
(D.D.C.), appeal dismissed. No. 19—5042, 2019 WL 1398194 (D.C. Cir. Mar. 
23, 2019), and affd, 920 F.3d 1 (D.C. Cir. 2019); United States v, Valencia, 
No. 517CR882DAE12, 2018 WL 6182755, at *7  (W.D. Tex. Nov. 27, 2018); 
United States v. Santos-Caporal, No. 118CR171AGFACL, 2019 WL 
468795, at *5  (E.D. Mo. Jan. 9, 2019), report and recommendation adopted. 
No. l:18CR00171 JAR, 2019 WL 460563 (E.D. Mo. Feb. 6, 2019); United 
States V, Castillo, No. 18-3579, 2019 WL 2061933, at *3  (3d Cir. May 9, 
2019).

Kirstjen Nielsen. Trump indicated that she would be succeeded by Kevin 
McAleenan, the commissioner of Customs and Border Protection, serving 
as acting secretary. In order to facilitate this transition, Acting Deputy
